sources.excerpt: The term “Chinese Restaurant Syndrome” originated from a letter published in the New England Journal

reasoning: Scientific consensus and rigorous double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have repeatedly failed to demonstrate a causal link between monosodium glutamate (MSG) consumed in normal dietary amounts and the group of symptoms historically labeled as "Chinese restaurant syndrome" (such as headaches, numbness, flushing, or sweating). The concept originated from a speculative letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1968 rather than clinical research. Major health and regulatory organizations, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the World Health Organization (WHO), classify MSG as "Generally Recognized As Safe" (GRAS) and acknowledge that studies do not support MSG as the cause of these symptoms under typical conditions.
title: MSG causes headaches — 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'
